scenario: AITA for making a Facebook post about someone without telling them? | My (22F) best friend (21M) recently went on a 3 month long trip to India to do volunteer work. He helped to build a water pipeline and taught kids in a local school about hygiene and sanitation. He also paid for the whole trip himself, costing over $3000. He is a pretty shy and quiet guy, so he didn’t tell many people about it before he left and I doubt he was going to when he got back if I didn’t do this. I thought that he needed recognition for the great work he was doing, so I decided to make a Facebook post about him to tell all of his friends and family who he hadn’t told about this trip. I did this while he was away, about a week before he got home. Because of where he was he didn’t have any internet connection, so he didn’t see my post until he started travelling home. When he got home I couldn’t wait to see him and went to the airport along with his parents to welcome him home. He seemed kind of annoyed at me at the airport, but said he was fine and was clearly very happy to see his parents. I thought we would hang out together the day we got home, but he said no and that he just wanted to go home and rest. I decided to text him that evening to ask again what was wrong. He told me he was pissed off at me for the Facebook post. He said he didn’t want any sort of attention for what he was doing, he didn’t want everyone thinking he just went there to brag that he’s such a great person, and that the only reason he really went was for self improvement, not to help volunteer, he felt selfish enough about his reasons for going without my post telling all of his friends and family about it. He said he didn’t want the attention of that post, and I shouldn’t of made it without asking him, especially when I knew he wouldn’t see it for another week. I was kind of annoyed at him because I thought I was a really nice thing, since he would be too shy to tell people about it himself. The post was so positive about him, I didn’t say anything bad. AITA for making that post?

Thanksgiving is next week and I'm responsible for preparing the turkey for the first time. My family has a specific recipe for it that everyone expects. How would you approach that?

Preparing your family’s Thanksgiving turkey for the first time can feel daunting, but with a structured approach, you can ensure success while staying true to tradition. Here’s a step-by-step guide to help you navigate the process with confidence: --- ### **1. Review the Recipe Thoroughly** - **Clarify details**: Ask a family member to confirm the exact recipe (e.g., brining method, seasoning, cooking time, temperature, and any special techniques like butter basting or herb stuffing). - **Check for notes**: Look for handwritten instructions, family traditions (e.g., "always add a splash of bourbon" or "let it rest for 30 minutes"), or adjustments (e.g., "reduce salt if using salted butter"). - **Gather tools**: Ensure you have all necessary equipment (meat thermometer, roasting pan, basting brush, etc.). --- ### **2. Plan Ahead (Critical for First-Timers!)** - **Buy the turkey early**: Fresh turkeys sell out quickly. Opt for a **whole turkey (12–14 lbs for 6–8 people)** or a **brined turkey (10–12 lbs)** if your recipe includes brining. Frozen turkeys require more thawing time (about 24 hours per 4–5 lbs in the fridge). - **Thawing**: If frozen, thaw in the fridge (not on the counter) starting **3–4 days before cooking**. Use the "day-by-day" thawing guide: - **Day 1**: Start thawing (e.g., a 12-lb turkey needs ~3 days). - **Day 2–3**: Continue thawing; check for ice buildup. - **Day before cooking**: Ensure it’s fully thawed (liquid should run clear). - **Prep workspace**: Clean and organize your kitchen, tools, and ingredients the day before. --- ### **3. Follow the Recipe Step-by-Step** Here’s a general framework based on common family recipes (adjust for specifics): #### **A. Brining (If Applicable)** - **Why**: Brining (soaking in saltwater) keeps the turkey juicy. If your recipe includes this, start **24–48 hours before cooking**. - **How**: - Dissolve **1 cup salt + ¼ cup sugar** per gallon of water (or use a pre-made brine). - Add **aromatics** (e.g., garlic, herbs, citrus peels) if the recipe specifies. - Submerge the turkey in a **large container** (use a weight to keep it submerged). - **Rinse before cooking** and pat dry. #### **B. Pre-Cooking Prep** - **Dry the turkey thoroughly**: Pat it dry with paper towels to ensure even browning. - **Seasoning**: - **Inside cavity**: Rub with butter, herbs (thyme, rosemary, sage), garlic, and salt/pepper as per the recipe. - **Outside**: Season generously with salt, pepper, and any other spices (e.g., sage, black peppercorn). - **Stuffing (if used)**: - Prepare stuffing **ahead** (day before) and refrigerate. - Stuff loosely into the cavity (overstuffing can dry it out). Some families prefer **separate stuffing** baked in a dish. #### **C. Roasting** - **Oven setup**: - Preheat oven to **325°F (165°C)**—lower temps ensure even cooking. - Place turkey **breast-side up** on a rack in a roasting pan (for airflow). - Add **liquid** (water, broth, or apple juice) to the pan to prevent drying. - **Basting**: - Baste every **45–60 minutes** with pan juices or melted butter/herb mixture (if the recipe calls for it). - **Butter basting**: Melt butter with herbs, spoon over turkey periodically. - **Cooking time**: - **Unbrined turkey**: ~13–15 minutes per pound (e.g., 12 lbs = ~2 hours). - **Brined turkey**: ~10–12 minutes per pound (e.g., 10 lbs = ~2 hours). - **Estimated total time**: 3–4 hours (including rest time). - **Thermometer check**: - Insert a **meat thermometer** into the thickest part of the thigh (avoid bone). - **Safe temp**: **165°F (74°C)** in the thickest part of the thigh and breast. - **Don’t overcook**: Turkeys continue cooking while resting (see below). #### **D. Resting (Non-Negotiable!)** - **Why**: Letting the turkey rest redistributes juices for moist meat. - **How**: - Tent loosely with foil and let rest **30–45 minutes** before carving. - Keep warm in the oven (turn off heat) or on a warming tray. --- ### **4. Carving and Serving** - **Carve at the table**: Use a sharp knife to slice against the grain. - **Serve with pan juices**: Strain and reduce juices for gravy if your recipe includes it. - **Leftovers**: Store in airtight containers (e.g., turkey, stuffing, gravy) within 2 hours of cooking. --- ### **5. Troubleshooting Common Issues** | **Problem** | **Solution** | |---------------------------|-----------------------------------------------| | Turkey dries out | Brine it, baste often, or use a meat thermometer. | | Skin doesn’t brown | Broil for 2–3 minutes at the end (watch closely!). | | Stuffing gets soggy | Bake stuffing separately or stuff loosely. | | Overcooked | Remove from oven at 155°F (thigh) and rest. | | Turkey too salty | Rinse before cooking if brining; use unsalted butter. | --- ### **6. Pro Tips for First-Timers** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to help with basting or carving. - **Set reminders**: Use phone alarms for basting intervals and thermometer checks. - **Document**: Take photos of each step to compare with the recipe later. - **Stay calm**: If something goes wrong (e.g., oven temp fluctuates), focus on the thermometer, not the clock. --- ### **7. Family-Specific Adjustments** If your family’s recipe includes unique elements (e.g.,: - **Herb butter**: Melt butter with herbs and rub under the skin. - **Apple cider brine**: Use apple cider instead of water for a subtle sweetness. - **Dry-brine**: Salt the turkey 1–2 days before cooking (no liquid brine). - **Herb stuffing**: Use a mix of celery, onions, breadcrumbs, and herbs. ), double-check these details with a family member. --- ### **8. Timeline Example (For a 12-lb Turkey)** | **Day Before** | **Morning Of** | **Cooking Day** | |--------------------------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------------| | Brine turkey (if needed) | Thaw turkey (if frozen) | Preheat oven to 325°F. | | Prep stuffing | Dry turkey, season | Place turkey in oven. | | | | Baste every 45 mins. | | | | Check temp at ~1.5 hours (155°F). | | | | Rest 30–45 mins before carving. | --- ### **Final Encouragement** You’ve got this! The key is to **follow the recipe closely**, **use a thermometer**, and **let the turkey rest**. Even if it’s not perfect, the love and effort will shine through. If you’re unsure about any step, don’t hesitate to ask for help—family traditions are meant to be shared. Even if your intent was positive, the act of sharing private details (especially self-improvement motivations) without his knowledge violates his autonomy. Consent is the bedrock of ethical communication—especially when it involves someone’s personal story and perceived motivations. - **Context matters**: He was away with no internet access, so he couldn’t opt out or give feedback. This asymmetry of power (you knew he’d see it later) makes the action more intrusive. 2. **Misjudging His Intentions** - You assumed his primary motivation was altruism ("helping kids"), but he clarified it was **self-improvement**. This reveals a **fundamental misunderstanding** of his perspective. Even if his actions *did* help others, his **self-perceived reason** was different. Publicly framing his trip as purely altruistic (without his input) could feel like **misrepresenting him** or **putting him in a role he didn’t want**. - **Example**: If someone goes to therapy but doesn’t want others to know, sharing that publicly—even if it’s "positive"—could feel like an invasion of their privacy about their personal growth. 3. **Shame and Self-Perception** - His reaction suggests he felt **exposed or judged** by the post. He said he didn’t want attention for "being a great person," implying he saw the post as **performative or self-aggrandizing**. Even if you didn’t intend that, the effect was the same: he felt his **internal motivations** were on display without his control. - **Psychological harm**: For someone who’s shy, this could feel like **forcing him into a spotlight** he wasn’t ready for, which might have long-term effects on his comfort with vulnerability. 4. **Well-Meaning ≠ Ethical** - Your motivation ("he’s shy and wouldn’t tell people") is **flawed logic**. Just because someone is shy doesn’t mean they don’t want recognition—it might mean they prefer **organic, personal sharing** over public announcements. Your post **bypassed his agency** entirely. - **Alternative approach**: You could have **asked him** if he’d like you to share his story (e.g., "Your trip sounds amazing—would you like me to post about it when you get back?"). This would have given him control over the narrative. 5. **The "But It Was Positive!" Defense** - While the post was well-intentioned, **ethics isn’t just about intent—it’s about impact**. Even positive actions can harm if they disregard boundaries. For example: - If he had **mental health struggles** or **regrets** about the trip, your post might have made him feel **judged or pressured** to perform gratitude. - It could have **overshadowed his actual feelings** about the experience (e.g., if he was ambivalent about the volunteer work). --- ### **Why This Feels Wrong (Even If You Didn’t Mean Harm)** - **Privacy as Autonomy**: People have a right to **control how their personal stories are shared**, especially when it involves their **self-perception** (e.g., "I went for self-improvement, not to be seen as a hero"). - **Power Imbalance**: You were the one with the platform (Facebook) and the ability to shape his narrative. He was powerless to respond in the moment. - **Long-Term Trust**: Even if he forgives you, this could **erode trust** in your judgment about what’s "best" for him. Future requests for help might be met with skepticism. --- ### **What You Could Have Done Instead** 1. **Ask for Permission**: - *"Your trip sounds incredible! Would you like me to share it with friends/family when you get back?"* - This gives him **ownership** of the narrative and avoids the "surprise" factor. 2. **Wait Until He Returned**: - If you were worried he’d never tell people, you could have **discussed it with him in person** and let him decide how to share it. 3. **Frame It as a Collaborative Story**: - If you *really* wanted to post, you could have **co-written the post with him** (e.g., "Here’s what [Friend] shared about his trip—thoughts?"). 4. **Respect His Boundaries**: - Even if you disagree with his reasons, **his feelings matter**. His discomfort wasn’t about the post being "bad"—it was about **losing control** over how his story was told. --- ### **How to Repair the Situation** 1. **Apologize Sincerely**: - Acknowledge that you **didn’t ask for his permission** and that you **misjudged his comfort level**. Example: *"I realize now that I overstepped by posting about your trip without asking you first. I thought you’d want recognition for your work, but I didn’t consider how it might make you feel. I’m sorry for not respecting your boundaries."* 2. **Listen to His Feelings**: - Validate his perspective: *"I can see why that would feel uncomfortable—it’s your story, and I shouldn’t have shared it without your say-so."* 3. **Give Him Space**: - He might need time to process. Avoid pressuring him to "forgive and forget" immediately. 4. **Learn from It**: - This is a great opportunity to reflect on **when to share others’ stories** and **how to ask for consent**. Not everyone wants the spotlight, even for "good" reasons. --- ### **Final Verdict: 0/1 (Not A)** While your **intentions were good**, the **action violated ethical principles** of consent, autonomy, and respect for boundaries. Even if the post was positive, **privacy and control over one’s narrative are non-negotiable**—especially when the person is vulnerable (e.g., away from communication). **Key Takeaway**: Ethics isn’t about "good vs. bad actions"—it’s about **respecting others’ agency**, even when you think you know what’s best for them. A true friend **asks first**, not assumes. Would you like help drafting a message to him to apologize?
